summary:
Still Here is a behavioral health support prototype for long-duration space missions. It combines shared family albums, weekly check-ins on connection, loneliness and perceived support, and guided peer support through Support a Crewmate.

Astronauts and loved ones build ongoing experiences together: a child shares a project, the astronaut contributes, and the child continues the story. Each contribution preserves their participation in everyday family life.

The project explores the relationship-support needs identified in NASA’s BMed-106 research gap. The current prototype demonstrates both perspectives in one browser, stores album pages locally, and simulates delivery after a connection interruption. Its effects on loneliness and well-being have not yet been evaluated.
details:
Our website is easy to use! Here’s how it works:

Open the site, browse the bookshelf and choose an album

⭐ Create an album with someone you want to stay connected to.

Select a page and add a photo and description

⚽Add a photo, a note, or a question that invites the other person to take part of the photo of your new achievement or a change of routine that is relevant for you all!

Share with family and friends

📷Tandan! Now the astronaut can share their thoughts on that important day! Continue the story together. Each contribution adds a new page.

Support a Crewmate!

Support a Crewmate is designed to help astronauts offer initial support to a distressed colleague. Inspired by Psychological First Aid guidance from WHO and the NCTSN/National Center for PTSD, it provides step-by-step suggestions for listening, offering practical assistance, and seeking medical support when needed. The demonstration content requires clinical review and is intended to complement crew training, without diagnosing conditions or prescribing treatment.

More about the project

The album lets each person record a moment as it happens, without waiting for the next call or writing an email. A child can post a photo of a paper rocket they are building at school. During a break, the astronaut asks how they plan to test it. After the launch, the child adds a photo showing how it went. By the time the next video call comes around, they have both taken part in the project.

Weekly check-ins ask users to rate perceived connection, loneliness and social support separately on a scale from 1 to 5. These exploratory self-reports are intended to help users reflect on their support needs and consider actions such as continuing a shared activity, discussing concerns with a trusted person, or seeking professional support. They are not diagnostic scores.
